newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-Indian arrivals indicate bumper crop.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Indian arrivals indicate bumper crop.

text.p: Increasing arrivals of Indian cotton in the new season, 1996/97 (October/September), point to a bumper crop for the second consecutive year, traders said on Thursday.
"It's rather early to estimate the new crop. But our expectation is that it'll be around 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kg), about the same as in the previous year," said a trader.
Daily arrivals at markets in the northern states of Punjab and Haryana averaged about 8,000 bales, against a trickle of 200-300 bales this time last year, he said.
"I expect the arrivals to hit a brisk pace of 30,000 bales a day by the end of this month," the trader said.
Traders said cotton production in Punjab, Haryana and the western state of Gujarat could add up to 8.0 million bales in 1996/97 against 7.1 million the previous year.
They said the standing crop in most states was good, boosted by late-September and early October rains.

The government has already authorised an export quota of 500,000 bales from the new crop and traders expect a further quantity to be released at a later stage to match the previous year's 1.59 million if not more.
In 1995/96, exporters signed up contracts for 1.1 million bales, traders said.
"Nearly 400,000 bales could not be contracted mainly due to late authorisation of exports last year," said a trader.
Traders expect domestic cotton prices to firm on renewed buying from mills ahead of Hindu festivals in the next one month, especially Diwali, the festival of lights.
Textile industry sources said they would expect credit controls on cotton trade to be withdrawn when the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, announces its credit policy on Saturday.
Cotton prices bounced back on the Bombay market in the week to Thursday, helped by purchases by state-run agencies, especially the Cotton Corporation of India.
In spot, Bengal-deshi (ready delivery) rose 150/190 rupees to 990/1,070 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned by 60/85 rupees to 1,660/1,730 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan moved up by 300/400 rupees to 12,800/13,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 by 400/500 rupees to 20,500/21,200 rupees per candy.
